facts.statement: Hepburn romanization (ヘボン式 Rōmaji) is the most widely adopted Japanese transcription system in international contexts, signage, and passports.
Standard Hepburn romanizes the five Japanese vowels as a, i, u, e, o, pronounced similarly to Italian or Spanish vowel sounds.
Hepburn romanizes palatalized or irregular consonant sounds phonetically for English speakers: し as shi, ち as chi, つ as tsu, and ふ as fu.
The voiced counterparts in Hepburn are じ as ji, ぢ as ji (or dji in disambiguation), ず as zu, and づ as zu (or dzu).
Contracted sounds (yōon) in Hepburn use y-combinations such as kya, kyu, kyo, sha, shu, sho, cha, chu, cho, and nya.
Kunrei-shiki (訓令式) is the Japanese government's official romanization system (ISO 3602), designed from a phonemic perspective: si (し), ti (ち), tu (つ), hu (ふ), zi (じ).
Nihon-shiki (日本式) is a strict 1-to-1 transliteration scheme mapping each Japanese kana row directly without English phonetic adjustments.

While Kunrei-shiki and Nihon-shiki reflect internal Japanese phonological regularity, Hepburn is preferred in foreign language teaching because 'shi', 'chi', 'tsu', and 'fu' match natural English pronunciation.
Long vowels in Hepburn are represented either with macrons (ō, ū) or circumflexes (ô, û); in casual ASCII typing, trailing 'u' or 'o' (ou, oo, aa, ee, ii) are commonly used.
A geminate consonant (small tsu / っ / ッ) is represented in Romaji by doubling the following consonant, as in 'nippon' (にっぽん) or 'zasshi' (ざっし).
When a geminate consonant precedes 'ch', Modified Hepburn uses 'tch' instead of 'cch' (e.g., 'matcha' for まっちゃ).
The moraic nasal ん is transcribed as 'n'; an apostrophe (n') is used before vowels or 'y' to prevent ambiguity (e.g., 'shin'i' しんい vs 'shini' しに).
Grammatical particles written with specialized kana readings are spelled phonetically in Hepburn Romaji: particle は as 'wa', へ as 'e', and を as 'o'.
Traditional Hepburn transcribes 'n' before 'b', 'm', and 'p' as 'm' (e.g., 'Shimbun'), whereas modern Revised Hepburn retains 'n' ('Shinbun').
Romaji is essential for Japanese input method editors (IME) on digital keyboards, where typing Romaji keystrokes converts text into Kana and Kanji.
While Romaji lowers the initial barrier for beginner learners, relying exclusively on Romaji obscures Japanese homophones and delays native kana/kanji reading speed.
Effective Japanese language pedagogy uses Romaji as a temporary bridge before transitioning early to Hiragana and Katakana.
Passport names and official Japanese road signs use variations of Revised Hepburn without macron diacritics (e.g., 'Tokyo' instead of 'Tōkyō').
